chunks: Among them is Amr ibn Hamama al-Dawsi, who lived four hundred years, and he is the one who says:

I have grown old and my life has become prolonged, as if I were healthy and stung by a snake for a night without being dismissed [from its grip]. Thus, death did not destroy me, but years of summer and spring followed one another upon me. Three hundred years have passed completely, and here I am, hoping for four [hundred].

key_terms.أَرْبَعَمِائَةِ سَنَةٍ: Four hundred years, the stated lifespan
key_terms.عَمْرُو بْنُ حَمَّةَ: Amr ibn Hamama, a specific narrator known for long life

ai.seo_question: Who is Amr ibn Hamama al-Dawsi and what is his recorded lifespan in Shia sources?
ai.summary: This narration from Kitab al-Ghayba highlights the phenomenon of long lifespans among Arabs, specifically citing Amr ibn Hamama al-Dawsi who lived for four hundred years. It includes his poetic reflection on aging, describing how he survived a snakebite without dying, allowing time to pass slowly through seasons, leading to a lifespan of three hundred completed years with hope for four. In Shia tradition, this account is often discussed within the context of *al-ghayba al-kubra* and the miraculous preservation of the faithful, serving as a testament to divine power over natural laws.
